lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
You finish class at 2:20. A bus leaves at 2:35 and 3:05. Which buses can you catch?

FEEDBACK
Both 2:35 and 3:05 (if you arrive by then); earliest sensible is 2:35.

WATCH FOR
Ignoring travel/buffer time makes an impossible tight plan look fine.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Build three daily plans using a timetable grid. Mark buffers and fix one overlapping plan.

Write a short reflection naming one step you corrected and why.

teach_steps.example:
WORKED MODEL
If Art ends 11:00 and Sport starts 11:10, you have 10 minutes to move. Choosing a 30-minute lunch starting 10:50 overlaps Art.

TRY FIRST
You finish class at 2:20. A bus leaves at 2:35 and 3:05. Which buses can you catch?

FEEDBACK
Both 2:35 and 3:05 (if you arrive by then); earliest sensible is 2:35.
teach_steps.explain:
Planning with timetables means sequencing events that fit without overlapping and that respect start/end constraints.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner choose methods based on place value, quantity and accurate working, rather than guessing digits by shape alone. Keep every step justified.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the places, values or distances that carry the method. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. Compare your working with the feedback: did you use the same skill and show your reasoning? If a digit or place is uncertain, identify what would have to be regrouped or counted again. One deliberate, justified revision is more useful than writing a longer answer.
teach_steps.notice: Ignoring travel/buffer time makes an impossible tight plan look fine. Correct the value or method, not just the appearance of the digits.
